title: The Courage to Name What Is
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer argues that speaking truth as a leader begins with naming reality clearly and calmly, not with opinion or outrage. She says people usually sense the truth but hesitate out of overwhelm rather than disagreement, especially when problems are large and have no quick fix. Her example is the aftermath of the Los Angeles fires, where she says many privately doubted that burn zones were safe to live in yet daily life resumed. Silence, she argues, is not neutral and costs individuals, organisations and communities. She reframes naming reality as an act of care and ends with reflection questions. It is a short, reflective piece that leans on one contested example.
points: Truth-telling in leadership starts with naming what is happening, without blame or drama.
Hesitation to speak is more often overwhelm than disagreement.
Silence is not neutral; it costs individuals, organisations and trust.
Grounded truth states what is happening, what is known and what must be considered, without demanding certainty.
quotes: In my own work throughout 2025, much of it focused on the issues laid bare by the Los Angeles fires, I was not surprised by the systemic failures that emerged. We have been living with them for a long time. What saddened me was something else entirely: the widespread unwillingness to slow down long enough to address them.
Most people sense the truth long before they are willing to speak it. They feel it in their bodies, notice it in patterns, and quietly adjust around it.
It wasn’t that people didn’t agree the challenges needed attention. It was that the problems felt too large, too complex, and too resistant to easy solutions.

Silence carries costs, to individuals forced to shoulder invisible risks, to organizations that lose trust, and to communities that sense something is wrong but are never given the language to address it.
Grounded truth is not about accusations. It does not rush toward resolution or demand certainty where none exists.
This is the courage required now, not louder voices, but clearer ones, coming together to reIimagine care for others as the foundation of our work, our leadership, and our society.
